name: Opsign
image_type: Opsign / pure actual optical situation (zeroness of the time-image, optical side)
definition: The actual visual image cut off from its motor extension: what is seen no longer passes into feeling or action, but stays on screen as a pure, de-differenciated optical situation that the look can only register. Together with its sound twin, the sonsign, it is the zero point from which every other time-image grows.
deamer_quote: ‘Everything returns to the purest zeroness – everything can begin again’ (p.138)
deleuze_examples: Europa '51 (Roberto Rossellini, 1952) - the bourgeois woman stares at factory workers: 'I thought I was seeing convicts'
Umberto D. (Vittorio De Sica, 1952) - the young maid alone in the morning kitchen, grinding coffee, looking at her belly
Stromboli (Roberto Rossellini, 1950) - the woman facing the volcano and the tuna catch
Late Spring (Yasujiro Ozu, 1949) - the still shot of a vase in a darkened room
L'Eclisse (Michelangelo Antonioni, 1962) - closing sequence of empty street corners
deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: A barnacled chunk of driftwood rolls in the surf at the tideline, breaks in two, and one piece drifts out of frame while the camera stays put.
A fixed camera on a stone seaside promenade with double railings; joggers, dog walkers and strollers cross, leaving the frame empty at times, until four old men with canes stop to chat.
Dogs sleep as dark blobs on a distant beach while the morning light bleaches sky, sea and sand into one white field.
The full moon reflected on black water at night wobbles and fades as rain and toads fill the soundtrack.

operation: Fix the camera on a place, object or onlooker where nothing is meant to happen and hold the image until what is seen stops leading anywhere.
shot_criteria: Judged on the image alone: a static or near-static shot of a place, object, light-change or crowd with no protagonist pursuing a goal, or an onlooker frozen in pure seeing; whatever moves (water, light, passers-by, animals) just happens and resolves nothing, and the next cut is not motivated by it. Sound is irrelevant to the test; the shot must hold with the sound off.
queries: driftwood rolling in shallow surf on grey wet sand, static camera, no people
static shot of seaside promenade with railings, strollers and joggers crossing frame, sea behind
dogs lying on a distant beach in overexposed hazy morning light
full moon reflected on dark rippling water at night
large flock of ducks waddling across a dirt path past the camera
empty city street corner at dawn, no people, black and white
woman standing still watching factory workers at machines, black and white
rain falling into puddles in an empty courtyard, fixed camera

name: Mirrors face to face
definition: The first crystal-image: one actual image splits into many perspectives through mirrors, reflections and doubles, so the body and its setting show up in fragments, duplicates and distortions, and you can no longer tell the actual from the virtual.
deamer_quote: ‘depicted space is complex, the body is a crystal’ (p.147)
deleuze_examples: The Lady from Shanghai (Orson Welles, 1947) - the hall-of-mirrors shoot-out
Citizen Kane (Orson Welles, 1941) - Kane walks between two facing mirrors, multiplied to infinity
Lola Montes (Max Ophuls, 1955) - the circus ring and its reflecting spectacle
The Golden Coach (Jean Renoir, 1952) - mirrors of stage and court
deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: On the subway Nina sees her own reflection in the blackened window, then through the glass doors between cars a double of herself in a black coat.
Nina warms up at a threefold standing mirror in the apartment's front room.
A communal dressing room of plate mirrors and small round table mirrors multiplies the ballet dancers.
The costumer's room makes almost endless copies of Nina; on opening night her dressing-room mirror is shattered and bloody.

operation: Put two reflecting surfaces into the shot so that the body appears more than once and one copy is not quite the original.
shot_criteria: A body or place visibly doubled, multiplied or distorted by a mirror, window, water or other reflecting surface inside a single frame; a plain unreflected figure does not count.
queries: woman looking at her reflection in a dark subway train window at night
ballet dancers practicing at the barre in front of a mirrored studio wall
theatre dressing room with rows of lit mirrors, performers doing makeup
person multiplied in an amusement park hall of mirrors
man standing between two facing mirrors, endless repeated reflections
face stretched and distorted in a funhouse curved mirror
clouds and trees reflected upside down in a still lake
cracked broken mirror showing a fragmented face

name: Limpid and opaque
definition: The second crystal-image: two sides of one image keep swapping places, so that as one becomes clear and visible the other goes dark, the way an actor turns into a role and back. The present is always passing into an opaque past.
deamer_quote: ‘An image is limpid – luminous, clear – for a moment’ (p.147)
deleuze_examples: The Golden Coach (Jean Renoir, 1952) - Camilla between stage and life: 'where does the theatre end, where does life begin?'
The Rules of the Game (Jean Renoir, 1939) - the chateau's masquerade and the actor's transparent and opaque faces
Lola Montes (Max Ophuls, 1955) - the circus reenactment of her life
8 1/2 (Federico Fellini, 1963) - film-within-film spectacle
deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: Six participants sit on plastic chairs in a bare warehouse while the method-acting coach leads them into their inner lives.
Lian plays King Lear alone to an empty theatre.
James is knifed outside his house by a gang of teenagers in his self-made short.
Ash's short turns violently brutal, so the 'real' Ash and the played Ash replace each other.

operation: Cut between a person rehearsing and the same person in the finished role until you can't tell which is performing.
shot_criteria: A frame that holds two states of one image at once: a person between self and role (rehearsal, costume, bare stage), or something visibly half-there (seen through translucent glass, fog, superimposition, or a screen lit from behind).
queries: people sitting on plastic chairs in a circle in a bare warehouse, rehearsal
lone actor in costume performing on stage to an empty theatre
actor in half-applied stage makeup backstage under a bare bulb
costumed players performing on a small curtained stage with painted backdrop
double exposure of a face superimposed over a city street
figure walking away and disappearing into thick fog
shadow play with performers silhouetted behind a lit translucent screen
shop window glass reflecting the street while showing people inside

name: Seed and environment
definition: The genetic crystal-image, oriented toward the future: a small actual object or moment contains a whole setting that has not appeared yet, or a large dispersed setting points back to a seed that can't be pinned down.
deamer_quote: ‘as if it were a miniature scene within a globe of opaque glass’ (p.149)
deleuze_examples: Citizen Kane (Orson Welles, 1941) - the snow-filled glass globe that drops from Kane's hand
Solaris (Andrei Tarkovsky, 1972) - the ocean as crystallising environment
And the Ship Sails On (Federico Fellini, 1983) - the ship as crystal in formation
The Leopard (Luchino Visconti, 1963) - the aristocratic world as crystal in decomposition
deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: At breakfast a children's TV cartoon shows farm animals learning about viruses: the seed of Caden's illness and of the play.
Caden rents a colossal disused warehouse and fills it with sprawling sets that grow into a replica of the city outside.
Adele paints tiny images that can only be seen through a magnifying glass, and they get smaller as she vanishes.
Old Caden with a cane walks through graffitied, ruined set-streets past a clock spray-painted on brick that reads 7:45.

operation: Show a small object that holds a whole world in miniature, then let the full-size world grow out of it.
shot_criteria: A shot where a small bounded thing (globe, model, seed, crystal, miniature, tiny painting, screen) visibly contains or foreshadows a larger environment, or a vast built environment that looks like it grew from one.
queries: hand shaking a snow globe with a tiny house inside, close-up
animated cartoon of farm animals and germs on a television screen
detailed miniature model of a city with tiny buildings, camera moving over
huge empty warehouse interior with stage sets under construction
crystals growing in a dish, macro time-lapse
painter working on a very small painting through a magnifying glass
bean seed sprouting and unfolding leaves, time-lapse
model sailing ship inside a glass bottle on a table

name: Peaks of the present
definition: The first chronosign: narration is laid out as several presents happening at once, each possible alone but not together (incompossible), so the story is no longer a line of successive actions.
deamer_quote: ‘the narration appears in the simultaneity of differing presents’ (p.153)
deleuze_examples: Last Year at Marienbad (Alain Resnais / Alain Robbe-Grillet, 1961) - incompatible presents of the man and the woman in the chateau garden
L'Immortelle (Alain Robbe-Grillet, 1963)
The Man Who Lies (Alain Robbe-Grillet, 1968) - the same event told in incompatible versions
deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

section3.film: Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives (Apichatpong Weerasethakul, 2010)
scenes: After the funeral, the family both stays in the hotel room watching TV and goes out to a bar to eat, at the same moment.
The ghost of Boonmee's wife appears, translucent, at the dinner table on the farm.
His lost son comes out of the forest at night as a furry monkey ghost with glowing red eyes.
Boonmee's dream of the future is told over still photographs of Thai soldiers with civilian-clothed prisoners.

operation: Show the same moment twice, happening in two ways that can't both be true, and don't choose between them.
shot_criteria: A single frame that holds two presents at once: the same person twice, split screen, superimposed people, clocks showing different times, or an ordinary scene with an impossible presence sitting inside it.
queries: family sitting on a hotel bed watching television in a dim room
split screen showing two different scenes side by side
same person appearing twice in one frame, trick photography
translucent ghost figure superimposed at a family dinner table
formal geometric garden with motionless people casting long shadows
wall of clocks showing different times for world cities
animal eyes glowing in a dark forest at night
still photograph of uniformed soldiers standing guard over civilian prisoners

name: Sheets of the past
definition: The second chronosign: the film moves around inside a pure past made of coexisting layers, jumping between them out of chronological order, with echoes and resonance taking the place of cause and effect.
deamer_quote: ‘There is no cause and effect, just events that ricochet, backwards and forwards’ (p.154)
deleuze_examples: Citizen Kane (Orson Welles, 1941) - witnesses' flashbacks, each a sheet of Kane's past; depth-of-field as memory
Hiroshima mon amour (Alain Resnais, 1959) - Nevers and Hiroshima as two coexisting pasts
Je t'aime, je t'aime (Alain Resnais, 1968) - the man jumping between moments of one year
Mr. Arkadin (Orson Welles, 1955) - an investigation through sheets of a man's past
deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: The narrator and the Marquis watch Peter the Great's chambers through dark glass and old stone, the Tsar's anger muffled and out of reach.
After a dark spiral staircase, a lateral track passes men turning wooden stage-wheels, soldiers in armour, dancers and an orchestra pit into Catherine the Great's theatre.
The travellers jump between sheets: Leningrad under siege, the Persian ambassador at court, Nicholas II's family at breakfast.
At the end the Neva has flooded and the Hermitage floats like an ark on the waters of time.

operation: Track one long unbroken shot through a building where each room belongs to a different decade.
shot_criteria: A shot through a space layered with accumulated time (palace galleries, museum halls, archives, storerooms, ruins, old photographs) where different pasts sit side by side, ideally deep focus or long tracking.
queries: long tracking shot through ornate palace galleries with chandeliers and paintings
visitors wandering through gilded museum halls hung with old paintings
grand ballroom full of dancers in period costume, wide shot
vast storeroom crammed with crates, statues and antique furniture
hands sorting through a box of old family photographs
children in the back seat of a car seen from behind, parents in front
bombed-out city ruins after the war, camera panning slowly
flooded city street with water around old stone buildings

name: Powers of the false
definition: The genetic chronosign, oriented toward the future: narration stops claiming to be true and works through series, repeating things with differences and letting fake and real bleed together, so truth has to be made rather than found.
deamer_quote: ‘no longer concerned with a pretence to truth, but instead with exposing this pretence’ (p.155)
deleuze_examples: F for Fake (Orson Welles, 1973) - the art forger Elmyr and the faked Picassos
Touch of Evil (Orson Welles, 1958) - Quinlan's planted evidence
Moi, un noir (Jean Rouch, 1958) - Abidjan dockworkers acting out their own fabulations
Pour la suite du monde (Pierre Perrault / Michel Brault, 1963) - islanders restaging the beluga hunt
deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: Static long-take interviews with Factory 420's workers facing the camera, some real and some scripted and played by actors.
Former apprentice He Xing remembers master tooler Wang among the factory's machines.
Little Flower tells how she was named after a Joan Chen film, and is played by Joan Chen herself.
The factory is to be torn down and replaced by the luxury '24 City' apartment complex.

operation: Film a sincere face-to-camera testimony, then give the same words to an actor, and never mark where the switch happens.
shot_criteria: A shot that stages testimony, copying or fabrication: people speaking straight to camera in a work setting, forgery or imitation in action, demolition to make way for a replacement, or identical things repeated in series.
queries: factory worker seated facing the camera speaking, machines behind him
old woman in a bare apartment speaking directly to the camera
tall factory chimney demolished and collapsing in dust
architect's scale model of new apartment towers on a table
artist copying a famous painting at an easel in a museum gallery
magician performing a card trick, close-up of hands
man being fitted with a false beard and wig by a makeup artist
rows of identical workers repeating the same motion on an assembly line

name: Bodies of attitude
definition: The first noosign: an everyday body shown in its postures, tiredness and habits instead of in action or imitation. The body comes before the plot and breaks up into many incompatible ways of being present.
deamer_quote: ‘Attitude describes a body that does not act, that is displayed in its complex everydayness’ (p.158)
deleuze_examples: Shadows (John Cassavetes, 1959) - bodies drifting through daily attitudes
Faces (John Cassavetes, 1968) - bodies worn down by waiting and fatigue
Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles (Chantal Akerman, 1975) - the daily routines of a body in the kitchen
Sleep (Andy Warhol, 1963) - the body filmed in its most everyday posture
deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: An eleven-year-old Black boy calling himself Woody Guthrie hops freight trains with a guitar case reading 'This machine kills fascists'.
Jude Quinn (Cate Blanchett) plays electric guitar with a band and shocks the folk audience.
Billy McCarty lives quietly as an old outlaw in an Old West town.
Jack Rollins, a folk singer seen in a documentary, reappears as a gospel-singing minister, Father John.

operation: Film the body between actions, waiting, slumping, fidgeting, and let several different bodies stand in for one person.
shot_criteria: A body shown in posture rather than purposeful action (sleeping, waiting, yawning, idling, repeating a chore, drifting through a journey), with its tiredness or habits visible in the frame.
queries: boy with a guitar case riding in an open freight train boxcar
folk singer with acoustic guitar and harmonica on a small stage
band playing electric guitars on stage in front of a crowd
old man on horseback riding slowly through a dry western valley
man asleep in an armchair, head nodding forward
woman peeling potatoes at a kitchen table, long static shot
tired worker yawning and stretching at the end of a shift
man slumped on a bench waiting in an empty train station

name: Bodies of gest
definition: The second noosign: attitudes are tied together and theatricalised into a ceremony or social gesture (Brecht's gest), a collective statement of the body that can end with the visible body disappearing.
deamer_quote: ‘The gest is that which links attitudes’ (p.159)
deleuze_examples: Le Lit de la vierge (Philippe Garrel, 1969) - bodies put through ceremony
Salome (Carmelo Bene, 1972) - the grotesque, theatricalised body
L'Amour fou (Jacques Rivette, 1969) - rehearsal turning bodies into theatre
Shadows (John Cassavetes, 1959) - gest as the link between attitudes
deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: Cristi, a plainclothes cop, follows the teenage student Alex through the town in long, uneventful takes of trailing and waiting.
At home Cristi eats his dinner while his wife plays the same Romanian pop song over and over, and they argue about what the words mean.
In Captain Anghelache's office the captain has a dictionary brought in and reads out 'conscience', 'law', 'police'.
The last shot frames only a whiteboard as the sting is drawn up; Cristi is no longer in the picture.

operation: Take an everyday body into a ritual (an office, a uniform, a ceremony) and hold the frame until the ritual has swallowed the person.
shot_criteria: Bodies turned into social ceremony or display in the frame: drill, uniforms, rituals, masks, mime, or official procedure (reading definitions, diagramming plans), with gesture shown as a public, repeated act.
queries: plainclothes man following a teenager along a city sidewalk, long shot
police officers standing in formation for inspection
official at a desk reading aloud from a large dictionary
hand drawing a plan with arrows on a whiteboard
carnival parade of masked and costumed figures in the street
mime with white painted face making exaggerated gestures
man eating dinner at a kitchen table while a record player plays
soldiers marching in step and saluting at a ceremony

name: Cinema of the brain
definition: The genetic noosign: thought appears in the mise-en-scene itself (sets, light, colour, sound) rather than in a character, and the world on screen becomes a map of the mind, a brain-screen.
deamer_quote: ‘The screen becomes an image of the mind’ (p.160)
deleuze_examples: 2001: A Space Odyssey (Stanley Kubrick, 1968) - the Star Child and the cosmos as brain
The Shining (Stanley Kubrick, 1980) - the hotel and maze as a mental map
Je t'aime, je t'aime (Alain Resnais, 1968) - the brain-machine experiment
Mon oncle d'Amerique (Alain Resnais, 1980) - lab rats and Laborit's neurobiology
deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: A god's-eye shot of Elm Street, with streets and houses drawn in white chalk on a black sound stage and labelled by name.
Characters in Depression-era clothes walk among real furniture inside chalk-outline houses, with a dog drawn on the floor.
The surrounding world is pure black or pure white, switching between night and day in an instant.
Invisible doors creak and characters knock on walls that aren't there while a narrator's voice runs over everything.

operation: Draw the town on the floor and shoot it from above, so the set works like a diagram of thought.
shot_criteria: An environment presented as a map, model or diagram of thought (chalk or outline plans, overhead grids, mazes, anatomy/neural imagery, cosmic fields), where the place itself is the subject rather than a backdrop for action.
queries: overhead view of a floor plan drawn in white chalk on a black floor
bare sound stage with minimal set pieces under bright lights
laboratory rat running through a maze filmed from directly above
animated diagram of nerve cells firing signals in the brain
aerial view straight down on a small town street grid
hand pointing along a street map with names written on it
rotating spiral galaxy against black space
X-ray of a human skull held up to a light box

name: Lectosigns
image_type: Lectosigns / the readable image (infinite of the time-image)
definition: The limit of all time-images: once images stop linking up naturally, frame, shot, montage, colour and sound have to be read and relinked by the viewer, and the film only exists through interpretation.
deamer_quote: ‘a film that not only demands to be seen, but requires a reading’ (p.163)
deleuze_examples: India Song (Marguerite Duras, 1975) - voices detached from the bodies on screen
Too Early, Too Late (Jean-Marie Straub / Daniele Huillet, 1982) - landscapes read as buried strata of history
Hitler: A Film from Germany (Hans-Jurgen Syberberg, 1977) - an image to be deciphered
Moses and Aaron (Straub / Huillet, 1975) - stratigraphic, readable image
deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: Oscar's DMT trip is six minutes of pulsating, morphing abstract smoke, fractal and kaleidoscope light.
From Oscar's point of view in the bathroom he splashes water on his face in the mirror; the shot comes back later reversed.
After death the camera floats overhead above the Tokyo night streets and neon, looking down.
In the coda, from the newborn's blurred point of view, a baby is born and presses into its mother's breast, then black.

operation: Take away every link between shots and leave the viewer to read the sequence like a text.
shot_criteria: An image that cannot be taken in at a glance and has to be deciphered: abstract light patterns, writing or text filling the frame, disorienting overhead or first-person views, or microscopic and organic forms that look like something else.
queries: abstract pulsating coloured light patterns, kaleidoscope effect
overhead camera gliding above city streets at night with neon signs
jellyfish drifting in dark water
red dye spreading and diffusing in a glass of water, close-up
printed page of text filling the screen, camera moving along the lines
man splashing water on his face in a bathroom mirror
newborn baby being delivered in a hospital delivery room
flower opening in time-lapse, close-up of stamens
